A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniPose and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. Their substantive material can be reliably matched despite layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original UniPose experiments across pose comprehension, generation, and editing, plus ablations and appendix retrieval/tokenizer evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports a Pose-ViT-only visual-encoder ablation.

M1.justification: The proposed pose tokenizer, dual visual encoders, mixed attention, training objectives, training stages, and inference procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same tasks, datasets, and evaluation scenarios, including the appendix LSP and multi-person examples. The added encoder configuration introduces no new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds Pose-ViT-only UniPose as an evaluated ablation comparator alongside CLIP-only and dual-encoder configurations. External benchmark baselines remain unchanged; PoseEmbroider appears only in Table 1's capability overview.

E3.justification: v2 adds a control with CLIP-ViT disabled to the existing two-epoch Pose Estimation/Image-to-Text ablation. Previously reported splits, metrics, training budgets, and other evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 6 previously compared CLIP-only with the combined encoders; v2 also tests Pose-ViT alone, isolating the contribution of adding CLIP. Other main-text and appendix ablations, robustness analyses, and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without adding repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The new Pose-ViT-only row in Table 6 reports MPJPE 96.3, PA-MPJPE 59.1, BLEU-4 12.5, ROUGE-L 31.0, and METEOR 34.8. Retained benchmark and appendix scores are unchanged; Table 2's 7,3-to-7.3 edit only normalizes decimal punctuation.

T1.justification: Equations 1–8 and their associated definitions and mathematical objectives are retained. No substantive assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the claims of unifying seven pose tasks, competitive performance, cross-task knowledge transfer, and zero-shot capabilities. The scientific scope of the abstract, introduction, and conclusion is unchanged.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanations, mixed-attention text-generation tradeoff, and Appendix E limitations concerning frozen visual encoders remain unchanged. The additional encoder result receives no substantive new interpretation.

D1.justification: v2's abstract newly reports code availability and supplies a repository link. Existing architecture, hyperparameter, hardware, training, and data-processing disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the PoseEmbroider reference and its capabilities to Table 1, acknowledging another method spanning several pose tasks. The remaining related-work discussion and overall novelty positioning are unchanged.

P1.justification: Limited copyediting corrects 'pose toke' to 'pose token', adds articles before dataset names, and standardizes H3.6M terminology. Section order and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 6 gain rows, spacing is tightened, and retained Figures 4 and 5 move to earlier pages as the main text reflows. Printed page numbers are removed. The illustrations and appendix displays otherwise retain their content.

improvement.justification: The added Pose-ViT-only control fills a focused gap in evaluating the dual-encoder design and reveals its modest advantage over Pose-ViT alone. The code-access link and PoseEmbroider comparison also improve documentation and context. These are limited gains; the method, principal results, interpretations, and limitations remain stable.
